utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Witness PW-161, we again would like to offer into evidence a document, which is a proofing note of April 21st, 2004, marked as 1D168, which was shown to the witness. Also we would also like to tender into evidence the March 20th, 2007 proofing note that the OTP offered us, which is 2D96; as well as the proofing-note letter from the OTP dated the 21st of March 2007; 2D86, and just if I can quickly explain the difference in the numbering. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is -- does it have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 2D87. And then we had also yesterday requested 2DIC79, which again was the issue with respect to the witness marking, I think he said volunteers; and then 2DIC80, which is where he marked the headquarters. And that would be our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Ostojic and I had a chance to talk about that and just the last -- the March 22nd proofing note makes reference to the witness's little chronology that he wrote himself out, so it -- it should be attached to it for completeness, and that he -- you may recall he acknowledged writing a little chronology out for himself. Otherwise, I think we're all set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment. I need to discuss something with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clarify this, Mr. Ostojic, and I'm sorry to ask you to stand up again. Yesterday for some time there was an indication that you wished to tender the parts from the witness's testimony in a previous case. You're dropping that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I covered it, with all due respect, quite extensively. I don't know, if the Court wishes to have that, we can break it down and give the Court the exact pages, but I think I cited it sufficiently and I think he answered it and I thought we showed it on a number of occasions, so I don't believe that it is necessary for our transcript. So I would withdraw that specific request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also wish to make it clear that that means that we will not have before us the transcript of his testimony in the other case. And although in some instances you read verbatim what shows in the transcript or various parts of it, in other parts you didn't, and you just referred to -- but you're leaving at that, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think so. If the Prosecutor felt that it was out of context, I'm confident he would have on re-direct have raised those issues, which he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we don't have a problem. As regards to the Ruez statement, Ruez interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Our policy is that we don't believe the interview should go in, generally speaking, Your Honour. We made an exception based on the Court's ruling. On the prior witness we made an adoption so the Court can see that the contact the witness prior to this one had with our client did not get mentioned at all. We thought it was significant. And this one, we thought we covered it quite extensively. If the Court wishes to have it, we don't have an objection to it. It's only 37 or so pages. Me and the OTP disagree a little bit on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, our position on the Ruez interview is the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have had discussions on this in anticipation of what you were going to offer for admission as Defence exhibits. And as I said in relation to the Blagojevic testimony, no problems. In regard to the interview, we have considered the totality of the witness's testimony, particularly when he tries to convince the Chamber that the interview by and with Mr. Ruez was totally confusing to him, and we need to know -- to have that statement in its totality to be able to assess whether -- how much weight we give to the witness and his statement that he was not following and he couldn't have possibly followed what Mr. Ruez was asking him during the interview. So what we suggest is that you tender this document in its entirety with the understanding that it will not be used as proof of its contents. In other words, the same line that we have followed in some instances before. Otherwise it will be very difficult for us to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That would be fine and we'll tender it as 1D167 as previously identified. I just want to make my position clear for the record. We don't believe the document should be introduced into evidence because it was extensively used. We think as we did with the prior witness, if there's impeachment, or for the purpose that the Court requested now, that documents or interviews should be allowed in, so I just want to make sure I draw a distinction between that, but we will tender it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I have the number, the 65 ter, or exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We marked it as 1D167, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So all these are being admitted. I think with the exception of the last two, which are the photos, that the witness marked, all the others need to be under seal. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We don't have an objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they have to be under seal. Because there is his name indicated in -- I think in all of these documents. So they are all so admitted. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's one other thing, if I may, Mr. President. So we're going to prepare that stipulation and present that to you, because I think he was vague in his testimony and on that one point we were stopped from asking further questions. We're not saying the Prosecution made the mistake and the Prosecution is and clear that he unequivocally changed it from one day to the another, and that's why we're offering those proofing notes, and I think we're going to get consistent with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with that and I think this is the simplest and most [sic] time consuming way of getting that point to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Least time consuming, sorry, least time consuming. Otherwise, the witness would still be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you both. Are there any other Defence teams that wish to tender? Yes, the Pandurevic team wishes to tender one document under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's 1D169, which is the testimony from the previous case. It's only at page 32, lines 8 -- line 16 to 22, which Mr. Sarapa put to the witness yesterday. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you to clarify this for us, please. The indication that we have here is that it is -- carries 65 ter number 1D169.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, that this is a document of the Popovic Defence team. Is 1D169 the entire testimony of the witness in that other case, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is. So I think we need to avoid confusion, because I don't want to have the entire transcript of the witness's testimony in that trial entered into the evidence, and I understand it will create problems for the Registry to -- so what I will ask you to do, and this will apply across the board to all parties in future, if you are only intending to introduce in the record a particular excerpt, a particular page or particular excerpts from a transcript of testimony in a previous case without wanting to introduce the entire transcript, then please try and copy and paste that part or those parts together in one document that you would then ask to be entered into the electronic -- e-court system that we have, and it will be given a name -- a number, and it will be that excerpts or those excerpts only that will be introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In that case, we will call it 7D305.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. 7D305.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it will be in e-court this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And yesterday we introduced, upon the request of the Popovic Defence team, 1D169, which is basically the transcript that I have been referring to. If you could kindly copy page -- the -- I don't want to mention the page, because it would reveal who the witness was. So the pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The number I was using was the e-court number, not the page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's because you are not wearing the headphones, Mr. Popovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. President, the mistake is entirely mine. I didn't appreciate that the whole of 1D169 had been admitted into evidence. I'm not going to put a separate piece of -- a separate passage of that transcript in and duplicate it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are -- no, no, no. I think you're misunderstanding me. What we are telling Mr. Zivanovic is what we told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he -- if someone might have been -- might have been carried away with the idea that the entire evidence, transcript of evidence of the witness in that other case has been introduced --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- so what we are asking Mr. Zivanovic to do is precisely what we asked you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you will copy on a separate sheet of paper, or sheets of paper, the excerpt that you wanted to introduce in evidence yesterday from that evidence, from that testimony, and it will be marked -- it will be given another number. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We were at cross purposes. I will then introduce 7D305, which will be that pasted passage and there will need to be a redaction of line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you follow me, Mr. Zivanovic? It's a simple operation, basically. You copy that part and introduce that part on a separate -- as a separate document and not as an integral part of the witness's testimony in that other case, yeah. It's simple, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Problem is that you didn't have the headphones on, and I think Ms. Condon was following exactly what we've been saying. Thanks. And we are redacting the reference to the page number from -- okay. I think that clarifies. Now, we will soon have in the courtroom Witness number 48. We agreed yesterday, or we intimated yesterday that we will be interviewing this witness and that before we go through that exercise, or begin that exercise, we would ask you for an input of the questions that you would have us put to the witness to decide whether to grant him the protective measures sought or not. So what I suggest is that we go into private session so that we hear what questions you would like us to put to the witness and then we can bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my part, I could do it in open session and would rather it was done in open session. I can't speak for others, of course. They may have rather more specific questions than the ones that am going to invite the Chamber to pose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that clarification. Is there any other Defence team that would be contributing in this context or not? I hear none. I see none. Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer. I see you somewhere -- somewhat bewildered or -- what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just one of those days, I think. But these questions in open session may themselves implicate the person's identity, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But -- I understand that, but also I give weight to Mr. Josse's good judgement. If it's not the case, in other words, if the questions that he suggests deserve to be heard in -- in closed -- in closed session, then we will redact and we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is the suggestion that the -- excuse me, that the -- Mr. Josse is going to be asking questions specifically to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think yesterday we made it clear that it will be more appropriate if the witness is interviewed by the Trial Chamber and not by the parties for the purpose of us deciding whether to grant protective measures or not. So my suggestion at the time was that of course you may questions that you would like us to put to the witness that you would put yourselves if you had that opportunity. I will give you the chance to tell us what questions you would put to the witness, and then we'll decide to -- to put those questions ourselves and we'll put them ourselves. This is what I suggested yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And at this time we're satisfied with the Court putting whatever questions it feels necessary, and if -- we'll let you know if anything in addition is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are relying on your good judgement. We will remain in open session for the time being, Mr. Josse. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course what we would invite the Chamber to do, as I'm sure the Chamber will do, is a general and careful scrutiny of the application. Specifically, what concerns as described in the motion amount to, and probe those concerns carefully and sensitively, whether the witnesses have received any actual threats in the past; in addition to that, what threats or actual violence the witnesses are fearful of in the future, and to probe whether those are real or fanciful. We would also invite the Chamber to examine with the witnesses whether there is any possibility, and I know this is rather unusual, that they might only require facial and/or voice -- facial protection and/or voice distortion. The real difficulty, so far as these witnesses is concerned and in particular 49, is the pseudonym. And that in particular is because a lot of 49's evidence would have to be in private session. So we would particularly invite the Chamber to see whether the fears of the witnesses might be allayed by facial protection, notwithstanding that their names would still be known to the public. Finally, Your Honour, we would invite the Chamber to allow counsel obviously on both sides to make submissions as to the evidence prior to the Court making any final determination as to whether or not to grant protective measures. Realistically, we need to be in a position to do that, we submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we had in mind in the first place, so I don't need to address that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, Your Honour. I think we both want the same thing, I'm...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Members of the public need to note that we will be bringing down the curtains for a short while. We will have a witness come in who is seeking protective measures, and we will need to interview him to decide if -- to grant protective measures or not, and that will be done in private session, in closed session. So it will take us some time before we can continue the proceedings in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse. There have been some similar cases in the past, and, fortunately or unfortunately, I had some of those. In some instances I made a suggestion to the parties, and they agreed to it, that in the absence of proper protective measures, certain safeguards be resorted to to allay, as much as possible, the concerns of the witness. In the past the instances that I am referring to, we resorted to the following measure, and that's again with the consent of both parties; Prosecution and Defence. Namely, that we try to do our utmost, without granting a pseudonym, to conceal the identity of the witness as much as possible. And that mainly involved two measures. One measure is not referring to him or addressing him as Mr. X during the course of examination-in-chief and cross-examination. And the other is to have him or the witness, I won't -- use gender neutral language, to have the witness sworn in private session. In other words, when he is asked for his name, surname, date of birth, place of residence and whatever, that's done in private session and then we will move immediately to open session and we proceed with the rest of the testimony in open session as much as possible. There may be occasions where we may need not to broadcast a particular document because it would immediately reveal his -- the understanding is that his name will appear in the transcript and in other words, it's partly hidden from public consumption, from the public domain, but not completely. We'd like to hear your comments on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I hope, speaking on behalf of all the Defence counsel, there can't be any possible objection to that. If any of my learned friends think I'm speaking out of turn, no doubt they'll inform Your Honour, but I can't see any difficulty with that, with respect, very sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Do you have any comments to make, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I think that sounds like a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me please confer with my colleagues, because we haven't actually decided to put in place in this system, not knowing what your response would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will be putting in place the procedure that you've kindly agreed to, and I think we need to explain to the witness two things. First, that he's not being granted the protective measures. Secondly, that with the cooperation of the Defence teams, there is going to be, in substitute, this kind of procedure. We will do that with the curtains drawn down for the time being and in private session. And then immediately after, we will revert to open session and lift the curtains up. Agreed? My apologies to the members of the public again, but you have to bear with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's break time. I didn't realise. Judge Kwon has just pointed out, drawn my attention that it is time for a break. So you will have a 25-minute break and so will we, and we will reconvene soon after and start with your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon once more. So, Witness, you have already made the solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. I don't think it's the need of repeating it, going through it again. Mr. Elderkin from the Office of the Prosecutor will be examining you in chief. He will be referring to a previous statement that you have made to the office, summarising it for us and for you. And then we will continue with some questions from Mr. Elderkin and finally cross-examination from some of the Defence teams. I don't think we will finish today, there is no chance of finishing today, so we'll try and I will encourage everyone to make it possible for us to finish with your testimony tomorrow. Thank you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Please may I start by asking to go into private session for just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you make a statement here on Friday of last week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that statement read to you in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you attest that the witness statement accurately reflects what you stated and that your answers would be the same if you were asked the same questions again today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer the witness's statement into evidence pursuant to 92 ter as P02486, and if I may read a brief summary of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could I ask just for the first paragraph that I go again into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being let's say yes and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In September 1991 he was mobilised into the reserve police forces, reporting to Zepa. In February 1992 he went back from Zepa to Rogatica. His family moved to Zepa in April 1992, where they lived with his parents. On the 21st of July, 1992, he fled from Rogatica to Zepa with the rest of the local population. In Zepa he joined the Territorial Defence until October 1992. Thereafter he returned to the police. Between September 1991 and May 1993, he had an automatic rifle. He surrendered the rifle to UNPROFOR. Thereafter he did not wear a uniform or carry a weapon. In 1992 and 1993 the living conditions in the Zepa enclave were desperate. The conditions improved after the arrival of UNPROFOR in May 1993 and a convoy with food came every week. In 1995, about a month and a half before the military offensive against the Zepa enclave, the convoys stopped. During the 1995 military offensive there was artillery and infantry fire into Zepa. There was heavy shelling all the time, especially from the north near Han Pijesak. The shells hit homes and the health centre; however, the Serbs did not shell the school because the Ukrainian Battalion (UkrBat) was housed there. The Zepa enclave was never fully demilitarised. Some people kept personal weapons, rifles and pistols. Zepa fell on the 24th of July, 1995. The transportation of the Zepa population started that night and continued until the 27th of July. The witness remembered VRS General Tolimir and a Serb officer named Pecanac both being present during this time. There was panic among the population; the people of Zepa feared for their lives. None of the Bosnian Muslim population dared to stay after the fall of the enclave. The witness was wounded in 1992 and his wounds became infected in June and July 1995. As a result, he received hospital treatment and could not carry out any police duties in July 1995. UNPROFOR doctors examined him, registered him and issued him with a certificate that he was wounded. For this reason, he was permitted to leave Zepa with the children and the elderly. He left on the last bus in the last convoy at around 11.30 a.m. on Thursday, the 27th of July, with 11 other wounded and sick men. The convoy headed in the direction of Kladanj. General Mladic came on to the bus at an UNPROFOR check-point at Boksanica and spoke briefly to the men. There was a long delay; sometime between 1900 and 2000 hours the commander of the Rogatica Brigade of the VRS, Rajko Kusic, came on to the bus and verbally abused the men. At 23.45 hours the bus set off again, arriving in Tisca in the early morning. At the last check-point of Tisca, a Serbian military policeman who was an officer came on to the bus looking for the wounded men. The witness saw him go to General Tolimir and get a list of the wounded and sick men. A police officer came back and told the men to get on to another bus. The they did so and were taken about 500 metres towards Vlasenica. They waited there for about 15 minutes and were ordered on to another bus that had arrived with the elderly. The witness heard that those elderly men had been robbed of their valuables by a military policeman. The bus went to the Rasadnik farm prison camp in Rogatica, arriving at about midday on the 28th of July. About 15 minutes later, General Tolimir spoke to the prisoners. He told them that a misunderstanding had occurred with the planned exchange of 48 Serb prisoners from Tuzla. He said that they would stay there for two to three days, but that there would not be any problems; no one would beat them and they had to abide by the rules. On the same day the prisoners were registered by the International Red Cross. The witness stayed in the prison camp until January 1996, during which time he and the other prisoners were abused. On the 11th of January, 1996, they were visited by the Red Cross and told that they would be exchanged. On the 15th of January, 1996, they were transferred to the Kula prison near Sarajevo, and on the 19th of January, 1996, they were exchanged at Butmir airport. Having read that summary, may I ask the witness just a few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, apart from your immediate family, your parents, wife and children, did you have any other relatives who were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had two other brothers and their families, so there were quite a number of close relatives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of your relatives, apart from the immediate family involved in the defence of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a certain sense all the inhabitants participated in the defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your relatives have any kind of command responsibility within the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of my close relatives did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you also the same with respect to your more distant relatives, insofar as they were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of my more distant relatives did participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask to go into private session for one question, it would speed up perhaps one point I would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see what the question is. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, what was the role of this person you mentioned, in the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask now what was your personal situation in June and July 1995. Were you working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June and July I wasn't working because my wounds had become infected and I spent most of the time in the clinic, since we didn't have a -- the traditional kind of hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you involved in any military or defence activities during the military offensive against Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether there was a process of demilitarisation when the UNPROFOR troops arrived in 1993 in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the enclave was completely demilitarised by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't completely demilitarised since some of the weapons had remained in the hands of the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did the inhabitants keep in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the whole, they had personal arms, light infantry weapons, hunting rifles, carbines, and perhaps the odd automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the number of people who were armed in the enclave in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be certain, but out of about a thousand fit for military service, I would say that between 30 and 35 per cent, at the most, were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the final military offensive against Zepa what happened to the weapons that the UNPROFOR troops had previously seized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day or two prior to the attack UNPROFOR returned the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I refer to one thing that you said in your statement: "It is hard to describe the feeling of panic that the people of Zepa felt. No one could stay in Zepa. No one dared to stay." I have one question regarding this. Can you say what it was that those people were afraid of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were afraid that they wouldn't survive if they stayed on there. That's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of anybody who did intend to stay in Zepa after it fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also in your statement you said that you saw General Tolimir in Zepa during the evacuations. Can I ask how you knew who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very difficult to provide you with a precise answer to that question. Perhaps I had seen him on TV or perhaps a member of his escort said that he was General Tolimir and that he was one of those participating in the negotiations with representatives of our government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Who is going first? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, you've just told the Chamber that you spent June and July of 1995 in the Zepa Hospital. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I spent a significant amount of time in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My second question was a clarification of exactly that, or along those lines. Did you at any stage during that period, prior to leaving Zepa, leave the hospital? And if so, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before the offensive I left the hospital and I went to my home to stay with my parents, where I had been living throughout that entire period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many nights before you left did you leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because it wasn't a clear question, I apologise. How many nights before you left the enclave for good did you leave the hospital? In other words, how many nights did you spend at your parents' before you left the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I spent about 15 days there in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So for most of July you were not in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of July, perhaps for the first 10 days I was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the fighting was going on in and around Zepa, you were not in the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first topic I want to ask you about is that very fighting, if I may. There was quite fierce fighting in and around Zepa in the second, third weeks of July of 1995, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the limited number of weapons that you say the Muslim defenders had, how were they able to defend the enclave so stoutly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to, because it was a matter of survival. They were fighting for their lives. The soldiers were fighting for their lives and for the lives of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, but I thought you told us that very few of the Muslim inhabitants were armed. My question is, without arms how did they defend themselves against the VRS attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, during the first few days of the attack there were no infantry attacks. There was shelling and attacks launched from a certain distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When I asked you a moment ago, "There was quite fierce fighting in and around Zepa," what did you think I meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You probably wanted to say that there was ongoing fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And "fighting" means fighting between both sides, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But when the infantry attacks followed, it lasted for two or three days and then all the lines fell, and that's how Zepa fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At this point, I'm not going to go into the detail with you, Witness, but it's right, isn't it, that the Muslim defenders defended the enclave in a strong and stout way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they couldn't continue to mount resistance. They defended the town to the extent that it was possible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask the question again, but that wasn't my question, and you knew it. You're deliberately not answering my question, aren't you, witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think it's getting argumentative with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my submission, it's a question and it's a perfectly proper question. It may be a strong question, but it's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a strong question. Perhaps you may rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on. I'm going to return to this subject later, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you saying, Witness, that the only arms that the inhabitants of Zepa had prior to UNPROFOR giving arms back were the few that you've already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not what I am saying and you will find this in my previous statement. Some of the weapons were brought by helicopters. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that was in breach of the agreement to demilitarise the enclave, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I had nothing to do with all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I dare say, but you were in the police force. Why didn't you do something to stop these weapons being delivered in breach of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army and the civilian police had nothing in common at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going develop this in the next few moments, but perhaps before I do that, prior to your entering hospital, were you still active in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never an active policeman. I was always merely a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you involved in any -- I'll rephrase the question. When was the last time you were involved in any policing activity in Zepa prior to your departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that this was in early June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what did you do for the police in early June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I performed the regular duties as an operative in the crime-detection police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may help to this extent: Paragraph 3 of your witness statement, and for this purpose I don't think you need to be shown it. It says, "In October 1994 I transferred to the criminal investigation department where I remained until the fall of Zepa." Is that sentence accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not fully. It shouldn't say I transferred, but I was transferred by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you don't need to worry about that. I'm not going to pick a dispute with you in relation to that and I accept what you've just said. Am I right to understand that sentence to mean that you were working in October 1994 full time in the criminal investigation department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you cease working full time in the criminal investigation department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June when I had to be hospitalised, and that was the end of my work down there, in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, it may be -- okay. Let me rephrase that question. Do you regard working full time in the criminal investigation department as being part of the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then I don't understand the answer you gave me a few moments ago where you said you weren't working full time in the police. Could you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that I had not worked full time. I said that I was not an active police officer, but a reserve policeman, which means that I had never been certified to perform the policing duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what practical difference did that make? Perhaps you can enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The difference lies in the fact that in order to be an active policeman, you had to be certified. You will have completed the police academy before you can join the police as an active policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me perhaps approach this a different way. What functions did you perform on a day-to-day basis when you were in the criminal investigation department from October 1994 to June of 1995? Tell us in some detail, if you need to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I helped, I assisted my colleagues who were active policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Come on, Witness, you can do better than that, can't you? What did these investigations that you were involved in consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never participated in any investigations. There was no need to carry out any investigations. There were no investigations at all. There were no crimes of that gravity that would require investigations to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Look, Witness, all I want to know is what you did at your place of work during that period. If it was sitting around drinking coffee, tell us. If it was some other function, tell the Chamber. That's all. Some detail, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no coffee at the time, so we could not be sitting and drinking coffee. There was a lack of coffee. For the most part I worked with a team involved in humanitarian aid. Let me explain. All convoys that were bringing food, that food would be stolen, so some of the goods would be missing. It was my duty to make a list of the goods that were stolen and I would submit that list to my superiors. As I've already told you, I assisted my colleagues who were active policemen when they were taking statements from people and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to the helicopter drops and the such like. Are you saying that that had -- that did not fall within the responsibility of the police, to detect these illegal arms drops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This might have been within the purview of the military police but not of the civilian police. The civilian police at the time did not get involved in that. It was not within their purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it might help at this stage, the civilian police were the SJB, and the military police was the SVB. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware that arms were being illegally smuggled into the enclave? Were you personally aware? In February, March of 1995, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody knew about those deliveries, including myself. But I did not know anything about the quantity of the weapons or the type of the weapons that were being dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At some time in early 1995 were you promoted within the Zepa SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you receive any sort of decoration or award for your services to the Zepa SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Approximately how many people, in 1995, would you say were employed by the Zepa SJB? In other words, how many police officers were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number was never fixed. It was never the same; there was a lot of fluctuation. However, the number ranged between 25 and 35 throughout all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 6D71? This document should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, this is a list of various police officers. The first list, for example, is of police officers who broke through along the Zepa-Kuti-Rubinici-Nevacka-Rudzicija [phoen]-Sokalina [phoen]-Ravne-Kladanj access. I'm not going to go through all the other documents. Perhaps we can go to the last page -- I mean all the other lists, but perhaps we can go to the last page where we see that the list at the bottom was compiled by Hurim Sahic. He was the Chief of Police, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You are welcome to look at this, but he describes in this document, which is undated but which, from its contents we can assume post-dates the events you are describing, what happened to various people who he describes as police officers and who presumably were under his command. Perhaps the Court would scroll through the document quite quickly for the witness. He simply needs to read, going from the top, what each list consists of, so he has some idea what I'm referring to. If we go back to page 1, please. He's seen the top of the page. Bottom of the page, please. You see the second list there, Witness, with four names. Top of page 2, please. Third -- on the second list says of police officers who disappeared in the break-through. Scrolling down we then have a list of police officers who were taken from a convoy transporting severely wounded and were taken to a camp in Rogatica. There's a name we're very familiar with at number 1, that's correct, isn't it, Witness? That is your name, it's not being broadcast. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then I think you've looked at the top of page 3 already. There are approximately 60 names on this list, Witness. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These lists also contain the names of the members of the reserve police stations in Luka and Krusev Dol in the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica. However, they were cut off from their own municipality and they joined Zepa. In other words, not all of these names belonged to the reserve police in Zepa, but also partly to Luka and Krusev Dol. That is why the list contains, or these lists contain so many names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which enclave was Luka in, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which enclave was Krusev Dol in, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also those are two neighbouring villages, but Krusev Dol is somewhat closer to Zepa than Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In Zepa itself, Zepa town, I'm talking about, where was the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the very centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the building called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building of the agricultural cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which other body or bodies was based in the building? Perhaps I can help you. The municipality was based there, wasn't it? The civil municipal authorities, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And also the premises of the Red Cross, the municipal authorities, and there were also one or two offices that were occupied by the army. Those offices were in the attic of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Colonel Palic's office in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was the commander of the 1st Zepa Light Infantry Brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have already made passing reference to the fact that the SJB and the Zepa Light Infantry Brigade did not get on terribly well. That's fair, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand was the source of the dispute between Hurim Sahic and Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really never gave it any thought. I was never interested in those things, to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you weren't interested because it was none of your business or because you thought the dispute was stupid? Why weren't you interested in it, bearing in mind that you were in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a simple reason: Those were probably their own private issues which then reflected on their respective services.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who were the civic municipal leaders based in the -- in that farm cooperative building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the municipality was Mehmed Hajric. The president of the Executive Board of the municipal assembly was Hamdija Torlak. Edhem Omanovic and Abdulah Piric represented the court, and I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea where Mr. Torlak stood in relation to this dispute between the army and the police? In other words, whose side, if any, did he take, as far as you could understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know. I never discussed the matter with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It might help and it might simply shorten this cross-examination, were I to ask you, did you hold any rank whatsoever in the police? Were you quite a junior officer? Where did you stand in the police structure, in other words? Can I stop you, if you want to answer that in private session, I've got no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was thinking -- precisely thinking of that. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who controlled entry and exit to and from the enclave? The police, the army, UNPROFOR, some other body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In spring 1995, I don't know in which month, I believe that it was either in February or in March, the only check-point was established in the Brezova Ravan sector. This is where both persons and goods were controlled, and in practical terms this was the only place where controls were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to dispute that. Who controlled it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did the power in relation to that lie with the SJB rather than the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that this must have been decided at a higher level of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you involved in any of the border control issues? Crossing-point control issues, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In what way, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were six groups of policemen who took turns up there. One shift lasted for four days. That's how long a group would stay up there. Which means that every 24th day I would go to that check-point with my group. That's when my turn would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about one specific incident, and that's perhaps easiest done by looking at 6D51. I see no reason why this document can't be broadcast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a report by a assistant commander for security, Senior Captain Hasanovic from the 25 -- 285th East Bosnian Light Brigade to the 28th Division command in Srebrenica. If we go to the bottom of it for one moment, you'll see who it's from, as I've just said. Let's go to the top of it, if we may, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You will see it's dated 31st of May, 1995, from Zepa. And I would like to go basically to the second half of the document, please, if we scroll down. I do have an English translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, no. Everyone else had except me, so there was something wrong in the system. So I've got it now, thanks to Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will read this, if I may, in English. And I'm pretty sure we've got the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "After this incident, the military observers," and it's clearly referring there to the UNPROFOR military observers, "halted their activities. They left the compound only twice, justifying their inactivity by a lack of fuel for their vehicles and the like. As far as we know in the meantime, the military observers have asked their superior command several times to be rotated. They were promised the whole team would be rotated, but this has not happened because the aggressor has not given them permission to cross over. Several times during regular briefings with the local authorities they asked the SJB to be allowed to leave, claiming that a new team of observers would come to Zepa the same day when they left. On 22nd May, 1995, the chief of the Zepa SJB, Sahic, gave the military observers permission to leave Zepa via Brezova Ravan check-point which is held and guarded by the Zepa SJB, and they used it to get out on the 23rd of May of 1995." I'm just letting the B/C/S interpreters catch up with my rather rapid speed, Your Honour. Witness, do you have any first-hand knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't. And believe me, this is the first time I've heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware that your chief had the power to control whether UNPROFOR military observers should and should not leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't think he had such power.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This document seems to suggest that he did have that power, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what it says, but I think that when it comes to facts, the facts were quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the very end of the same document, the last paragraph, I beg your pardon, the last sentence, in fact, follows a passage which describes the animosity between the SJB chief and the 285th Light Infantry Brigade commander and then it says, "However, cooperation between the SVB and the SJB has recently begun to change thoroughly and radically for the better, even though cooperation is still disrupted by the autocratic behaviour of the chief of the Zepa SJB, because it was realised that cooperation was indeed necessary." Do you agree that in late May of 1995 cooperation between the SJB and the SVB improved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even if there was such cooperation, it wasn't obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were in the police. Do you accept Mr. Hasanovic's description of the chief of the Zepa SJB as "autocratic" -- I beg your pardon, his behaviour as being autocratic? Do you accept that as an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree with that, and this is really very funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why is it funny, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, given that he found such a term, given that he expressed himself by using such a term.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Move on to another related topic. The authorities in -- within the enclave were not keen on people leaving the enclave in the first part of 1995, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the military observers and to their departure?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wasn't, but let's deal with them first of all. Why were the authorities not keen for the military observers to depart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, while they were present there was a form of security and we felt that there would be no new attacks and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Now, my question, and my apologies for not making it clear in the first place, was directed to efforts by the authorities, civic, military and police, to prevent the civilian inhabitants from leaving the enclave during the first part of 1995. Would you agree with the proposition that efforts were made to stop people leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one even tried to prevent anyone from doing so. There was an agreement, this was the result of negotiations, on the civilian population leaving the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were efforts made to stop members of the police force from leaving the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were efforts made to stop members of the 1st Zepa Light Infantry Brigade from leaving the enclave, in other words deserters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I want to have a look at a few documents with you, if I may. First of all, 6D97. This is another army document. It's from Assistant Security Commander Nedzad Bektic from the Srebrenica 8th Operation Group. It's headed, "Prevention of illegal abandonment of the Srebrenica 8th Operation Group." If I could read a little bit of it out, "There has recently been an increase in the --" it's translated as "number of people illegally leaving the zone of responsibility of the 28th Division of the Srebrenica 8th Operation Group going in the direction of Luka-Slap and further towards Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia. Since the crossings are taking place in the area of responsibility of the 285th Brigade and judging by the manner in which they are carried out, there are grounds to suspect the crossings are organised and carried out in cooperation with the enemy." And then it deals with the measures that need to be taken to stop this. Your reading of the document, Witness, does this refer to soldiers, civilians, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So I repeat what I asked you a moment ago. Were you aware at the time that this was an issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially nothing had been discovered, nothing had been seen, but there were rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Rumours to what effect? What were those rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rumours to the effect that the events mentioned had happened, but officially nothing had been discovered, nothing had come to light with regard to whether there was really cooperation with the enemy with regard to those who were involved in planning, organisation and who perhaps moved over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why were the army keen to prevent civilians leaving the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should ask someone from the army, someone who has information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, sadly, I don't think I'm going to have the opportunity to in this particular case. That's why I'm asking you, but if you don't know the answer, that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that towards the bottom of the document we see it says, "The brigade commander and assistant commander for security shall be responsible for carrying out these tasks and the Zepa public security station shall also be involved." That's what the document says. No dispute about that, I'm sure. Were the Zepa public security station, of which you were part, involved in stopping this so-called illegal activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I am aware. I don't know whether they were at all informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the next document, please, which is 6D47. And take it from me that this is clearly a reply by Captain Hasanovic to the last document, because the reference number matches that on the document I have just shown you. This is dated the 5th of February, 1995; six days later, in other words. And I'll read a little bit. It says, "I immediately took certain steps and measures to find and identify persons who leave the territory without authorisation, as well as the organisers of these activities. In this work I have also engaged the Zepa SJB and the Luka police station." But you've got no recollection or knowledge of that happening. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the document it talks about temporary permits being issued to those who come here for food so that they can leave the territory of Srebrenica with some kind of official document. Any knowledge of that happening; permits being issued to people who were after food or the such like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such permits were issued, but only for those who had come from Srebrenica to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other document in this regard that I'd like to show you. 6D39, please. We are now going up rather higher in the chain of command, and here we have an instruction sent from Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic to Colonel Palic personally. We're also getting far nearer the time that we're particularly interested in, 26th of May, 1995, so far as this document is concerned. It says, "In order to prevent certain civilians and any members of the BH Army from leaving the territory of Zepa without permission and illegally, it will be necessary to exercise the following measures: In cooperation with the SJB, create a plan to prevent the townspeople of Zepa from leaving for other territories." And then there is other measures which, so far as you're concerned, we don't need to go into. You are still saying you had no knowledge of orders coming from the very highest ranks of the establishment of the ABiH to prevent both soldiers and civilians from leaving your enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Last question on this. Can you think of any reason why Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic would want to stop civilians leaving the enclave of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't even start guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a little bit about the trade the other way, so to speak. Things that were being smuggled into the enclave. And I don't mean by that weapons, because you have accepted that weapons were being smuggled in. Were you aware of fuel being smuggled in to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How was that done, please? To the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At all UNPROFOR check-points fuel would be sold. They would sell fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Illegally; is that what you're saying? UNPROFOR would create a black market in fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They sold it illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what services, goods, or other things did the inhabitants of Zepa pay the UNPROFOR troops with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They paid in cash and alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Cash being Deutsch marks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and dollars, if anyone had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you one -- or to direct you to one specific document in relation to the smuggling of fuel. Could we have a look at 6D72, please. This is a -- as it's being brought up, I can perhaps introduce it -- a Serb-generated document. It's from a Colonel Andric, commander of the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade, dated the 12th of May, 1994 -- 5, I beg your pardon. Order to prevent smuggling of fuel by UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other organisations. "We have received information that members of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other international organisations have been transporting fuel illegally to Muslims in the enclaves of Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa and Srebrenica. They smuggled fuel in double or large tanks on combat and non-combat vehicles which they empty in the enclaves, leaving just the quantity needed for their return journeys from the enclaves to the territory of the FRY or the RS." Any knowledge of that specific activity, the activity described in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, UNPROFOR received the amount that they requested or that they needed. I'm referring to their own needs. And they sold a certain amount of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This document, I would suggest, relates specifically to the smuggling of fuel in double tanks. If we look at item number 5, perhaps you could scroll down, it actually says, "Treat the fuel from double tanks and other secret storage areas as smuggled, confiscate it and enter it in the books of your battalion." My question is, were you aware of smuggling with the use of double tanks and other secret storage areas on or within a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat that answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, the interpreters have asked if you could repeat what you have just said, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't provide a concrete answer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of smuggling by use of double tanks or other secret storage areas within vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no one even checked those vehicles then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like to go back, as I said that I would, to the fighting within the enclave. You have told us that for the -- excuse me, I can't remember -- I think you said 10 days before your departure you were at your parents' home. You've also told us that you were aware of the fighting going on around you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where the communication centre, used by the defenders of the enclave, was situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the Zepa mountain area, but I don't know where the exact location was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was it -- at what point in time was it first situated in the Zepa mountain area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where it was located when it was moved from the centre of Zepa to the mountain. Well, I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me but, in fact, there are two questions I now want to ask in relation to this. The first is, do you know when it was moved from the centre of Zepa to the mountains? Approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either when the attack had already started or immediately prior to the attack, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to the communication centre being moved to the mountains, immediately prior, I'm talking about, where in the centre of Zepa was it situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the building in which Palic had his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which was the farm cooperative building; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So your understanding is it was moved from the farm cooperative building to the mountains and was never situated anywhere else within the town itself at the material time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's see if I can jog your memory. Let's have a look at 6D81. We see that this is a document from the 285th East Bosnian Light Brigade to the 28th Division. Could we go to the bottom of the document for a moment, please, and see who the author is? Second page. We see that the author is chief of communications, Alija Gusic. Was that someone you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go to item number 5 of this report dated the 2nd of July, 1995, time 1830. If you would be so kind, Witness, I think I'll ask you to read this. Read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the English interpreters do not have the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry. I have just received a message from the English interpreters that they don't have the English text. It will be easier if I read it in English, because the B/C/S translators will be able to see what you can see, so I'll read it. "There were no immediate problems in work. The minor problem is the fact that we had to move the CV to the hospital basement because of enemy shelling and quality of transmission is now poor." What do you understand by the initials "CV"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose this is the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that, Witness. It was moved to the place that you were residing, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to that place, but to the same building. He was in the basement, and I was one floor above.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many patients were there in the hospital at the beginning of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not more than three to four.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were any of the other patients police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And is your evidence to this Trial Chamber that you didn't know that the communications centre of the Zepa Brigade had been moved to the very place that you were residing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You didn't see Mr. Gusic coming in and out of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have done, but we didn't -- did not use the same entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so I suppose it will be futile for me to ask you why it was the army chose to place the communications centre in the hospital. You wouldn't know, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, and thank you, Mr. Josse. Let's proceed. Please allow something like five, seven minutes towards the end for us, because we need to hand down an oral decision and also give you some information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, having had the break to reflect, I'm going to go back in time, if I may, in relation to one document. Let's go straight to it. It's 6D49. And this, in fact, is a long series of documents, headed,"The public security station in Zepa" dated the 5th of February, 1995, to the ministry of the interior of the RBH and the introduction basically says that there follows a collection of documents in relation to a particular topic. The first of this collection of documents, we can just see the top of on the screen at the moment. It's dated the 30th of October, 1994. And take it from me, Witness, the bottom of that document, it's signed by the chief of the Zepa SJB, Hurim Sahic. And there are two or three parts of this document that I would like to ask you about. Much of it, to summarise, is a complaint by the Chief of the Police about the behaviour of Colonel Palic, and you've already alluded to the fact that you knew of it but didn't know what it was about. At the very bottom of that first page it says, "The soldiers from what is known as Avdo's delegation, are spreading all --" and please turn the page in the B/C/S, or scroll down -- "All kinds of information, some of which was voiced at a meeting of the local brigade staff here when they gave a briefing on their visit to Sarajevo. It was said that the military had the main role in Zepa and the civilian organs and the president of the municipality were there only for show for the UN and UNPROFOR, that everything was subordinated to Commander Avdo Palic, that he made all the decisions, that the Zepa SJB should be abolished and its role taken over by the military police and the sabotage units." So, to remind you, this was the 30th of October of 1994. Can you comment on what your chief is saying there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no comment. Such things happened, but who did them, who issued orders, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, is what Mr. Sahic is saying true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Little further down the page, yes, that's fine, it's there. It says, "The various forms of disinformation spread by the people from Avdo's delegation have had repercussions on the situation in the Zepa SJB, particularly information on the disbanding of the Zepa SJB, as well as information that so far, the 1st Zepa Light Brigade has received around 4.000 Deutsche marks and that this money is for the exclusive use of the brigade --" 400.000, I'm sorry. Thank you. "And that this money is for the exclusive use of the brigade and its members while other organisations in Zepa have no resources at their disposal." Firstly, are you aware that Colonel Palic wanted to disband the Zepa SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only did he want to do that, he actually insisted on this being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't go into the reasons because I don't know what the reasons for that were. I'm sure he would be able to tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he succeed in disbanding the Zepa SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't. It remained in place because it provided services for the civilian population. That's why it had been established in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have no idea what Colonel Palic's complaint was with the body you worked for. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the 400.000 Deutsche marks? Is it true that he received -- the brigade received that money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be a hundred per cent sure. I know that some money came, but I don't know how much, how that money was used, on what, I really can't tell you that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we go to the third page of the document we see there numeral 1, it says, "In October, 1993, on his way back from Sarajevo, as a member of the Zepa delegation, the commander of the aforementioned brigade stole 5.000 Deutsche marks from the money which he was bringing to the Zepa War Presidency." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An investigation was carried out by the security officers from the brigade. I don't know what they found. This information never left the army circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's all very well you're saying that. But this is an SJB document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So your chief knew about it, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (expurgé) (expurgé) (expurgé) (expurgé) (expurgé) (expurgé)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's do it even better. I suggest that we redact also your question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I've got no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will redact the question from line 15 to line 19 -- to line 20. And we go to private session now. In private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's one other part of this document I'd like to ask you about. And we need to go to the bottom of the second page in the B/C/S. The middle of the third page in the English. It says, and I'll read it slowly so that you can find the place. "The only developments that excited the population were a conflict between the commander of the local brigade and the command of the operations group about the way the Luka Company operated."
